list.listitem: Risk factors for oropharyngeal (OP) cancer include tobacco and alcohol use as well as human papillomavirus (HPV) infection. B
Suspect OP cancer in patients with an OP mass or ulceration, or suspicious cervical lymphadenopathy. C
Tissue biopsy is required to determine a pathologic diagnosis. C
Local or locoregional disease is most often treated with curative intent with either radiation alone or concurrent radiation and chemotherapy. A
Patients presenting with metastatic disease may benefit from systemic chemotherapy, local radiation to palliate symptoms, or both. B

background.definition: Oropharyngeal (OP) cancer is defined as a primary tumor arising from the soft palate, base of tongue (posterior one third), vallecula, or pharyngeal wall below the nasopharynx and above the larynx.

list.listitem: There were an estimated 12,660 new cases of cancer in the pharynx in 2010 in the United States.
While the National Cancer Institute does not breakdown these statistics further, it has been shown that approximately 62% of pharyngeal cancers are found in the oropharynx.
While the overall rate of smoking is decreasing, there has not been a concomitant decrease in OP cancer.
There is a male predominance (2:1).
Tobacco and alcohol exposure leads to malignant transformation of squamous epithelia.
It has been proposed that HPV infection and expression of viral proteins E6 and E7 also lead to cell transformation.
The increase in HPV-positive tumors in younger, nonsmoking patients also suggests an etiologic role for HPV infection.
Evidence of HPV infection can be found in as many as 57% of patients with OP cancer.
Greater than 95% of OP cancers are squamous cell carcinomas and spread primarily through the lymphatics and secondarily through hematogenous dissemination.
Nodal involvement is seen at presentation in half or more of patients. The most common site of nodal involvement is the ipsilateral level II node (ie, jugulodigastric).
Less than 20% of patients have metastasis at initial presentation. Common sites of metastasis include nonregional lymph nodes, lung, and bone.

The United States Preventive Services Task Force updated recommendation in 2013 concluded that evidence was insufficient to recommend screening for oropharyngeal cancer. A Cochrane review identified a single large cluster-randomized trial found a possible mortality benefit in high risk individuals in India, but was felt to be at high risk of bias.

A systematic review of 8 studies of the clinical examination to screen for oral lesions found that it was relatively sensitive and very specific. Whether screening results in better outcomes is not known, though.C
Suspect OP cancer or other head and neck cancer in patients with dysphagia or a change in voice quality or strength. C
When patients are found to have positive cervical lymph node(s) with occult primary, the tonsillar fossa and base of tongue are the most likely sites. B
Staging is based on the physical examination, direct laryngoscopy, and imaging with diagnostic CT or PET/CT scans.C
The final diagnosis requires pathologic evaluation. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Nonfixed, "rubbery" neck mass with negative biopsy
Biopsy positive; cytokeratin (carcinoma) or leukocyte common antigen (lymphoproliferative)

list.listitem: Patients are staged according to AJCC criteria: Stage I: Tumors less than or equal to 2 cm with no regional or distant spread (T1,N0). Stage II: Tumors less than or equal to 4 cm and greater than 2 cm with no regional or distant spread (T2,N0). Stage III: Tumors greater than 4 cm with no regional or distant spread (T3,N0), or tumors of any size with one ipsilateral lymph node that is 3 cm or less in diameter (T1-3,N1). Stage IVA: Tumors that extend into neighboring structures but still generally resectable (ie, larynx, extrinsic muscles of tongue, medial pterygoid, hard palate, or mandible [T4a,N0-2]), or metastasis to a single ipsilateral lymph node greater that 3 cm but not greater than 6 cm (T1-4a,N1a), or metastasis to multiple ipsilateral lymph nodes (T1-4a,N1b), or metastasis to contralateral lymph node(s) (T1-4a,N1c). Stage IVB: Tumors that extend into deeper or more vital structures and are not resectable (lateral pterygoid muscle, pterygoid plates, lateral nasopharynx, or skull base or encases carotid artery [T4b,N0]), or metastasis in a lymph node more than 6 cm in its greatest dimension (T1-4b,N3). Stage IVC: distant metastasis (M1).

Patients with OP cancer commonly present with hoarseness or dysphagia. They may also have a muffled or 'hot potato' voice, but any change in voice quality or strength should prompt evaluation for laryngeal involvement.
In a retrospective study of 221 upper aerodigestive tract neoplasms, the presenting symptoms was hoarseness in 28%, throat pain in 20%, change in the tongue in 11%, and tongue mass in 10%.

OP tumors are identified by visualization and palpation. Digital palpation of the base of tongue, vallecula, and tonsillar fossa can aid in identifying the extent of disease. Tongue atrophy, fixation, or deviation suggests deep invasion of the musculature (T4 disease).
Referred otalgia is common and results from compression of cranial nerves IX or X.

An enlarged (>1 cm), hard or fixed cervical node in an adult is malignancy until proven otherwise. Node size should be documented to evaluate for progression. Cervical lymphadenopathy suggests a head and neck primary site such as the oral cavity, oropharynx, nasopharynx, hypopharynx, or larynx. The tonsillar fossa and base of tongue, subsites of the oropharynx, are the most likely areas of occult primary in the United States. Skin, salivary glands, and thyroid gland are less common sites of origin. Supraclavicular lymph nodes may also suggest lung or esophageal primary sites. Left supraclavicular lymphadenopathy may suggest metastatic disease originating from below the diaphragm.
Axillary lymphadenopathy, lung nodules, or focal bone pain in the setting of a primary head and neck cancer suggests the presence of metastatic disease.
A clinical screening examination by a physician is fairly sensitive and very specific for oral cancer or precancer.
Perform direct pharyngolaryngoscopy with biopsy to determine the location and sites of involvement, tumor size for staging, and to establish a pathologic diagnosis.
Order CBC and a comprehensive metabolic profile. Low hemoglobin confers poor prognosis.
Elevated AST/ALT or alkaline phosphatase is concerning for liver metastasis but has not been shown to be a reliable predictive factor.

CT scan of the neck with IV contrast enables appropriate staging according to AJCC criteria. PET/CT imaging has greater sensitivity for identifying metastatic disease. MRI can be considered to evaluate for muscle invasion as well as for skull base involvement in the setting of cranial neuropathy.
Presentation with a neck node and no visible primary site should be evaluated with imaging as well as direct laryngoscopy with ipsilateral tonsillectomy and random biopsy.
Consider complete dental evaluation for possible tooth extraction prior to therapy.
Patients with dysphagia or change in voice should undergo initial testing with direct laryngoscopy.
Patients with OP mass or suspicious lymphadenopathy should have a biopsy performed to establish a pathologic diagnosis.
Lymph node biopsy should be performed by fine needle aspiration or core biopsy. Open biopsy is discouraged as it can complicate definitive therapy.
Curative treatment for OP cancer typically consists of radiation therapy or radiation therapy in combination with chemotherapy. ASurgery may be an alternative approach for selected patients. C
Patients presenting with metastatic disease may benefit from local radiation therapy or systemic chemotherapy.C

Concomitant radiation and platinum chemotherapy following surgery are more effective than radiation alone after surgery. A Cochrane systematic review identified 100 trials and over 18,000 patients to assess the efficacy of chemotherapy in managing oropharnygeal cancer. Adjuvant chemoradiation after surgey reduced the risk of death by 16% compared to adjuvant radiation alone after primary surgery

The same Cochrane review was unable to demonstrate any benefit for induction chemotherapy prior to surgery or radiation. However, if radiation was being given as primary treatment then the addition of concurrent chemotherapy improved overall survival compared to treatment with primary radiation alone (HR 0.74, 2852 patients).

A study compared concurrent paclitaxel and cisplatin plus a reduced total dose of radiotherapy to standard fluorouracil-cisplatin based chemotherapy plus conventional radiotherapy. Disease free survival was lower in the paclitaxel group.

There is not sufficient evidence to support use of cetuximab in combination with platinum. Cetuximab may be used in combination with radiotherapy in fit patients who are not candidates for platinum but as single agent is less effective than radiotherapy with platinum.

A study identified 182 patients with HPV associated oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma (stage III excluding T1-2N1 or stage IV excluding T4 and/or N3 and/or N2b-c if smoking history >10 pack years and/or distant metastases). They were randomized to radiation therapy with either weekly cisplatin (7 doses of 40 mg/m2) or cetuximab (loading dose of 400 mg/m2 followed by 7 weekly doses of 250 mg/m2). Cetuximab was inferior to cisplatin with a 3 year failure-free survival rate of 80% vs 93% (p = 0.015).

A study randomizing 80 patients with recurrent or metastatic head and neck squamous cell carcinoma found that adding cetuximab to temsirolimus did not significantly improve progression free survival. However, the study may have been underpowered.

The addition of immunotherapy with nivolumab to standard treatment in recurrent head and neck cancer can modestly improve overall survival. In a trial of 361 patients, the median overall survival was increased by 2.4 months and progression free survival at 6 months was 20% vs 10% with placebo.

An RCT of almost 500 patients with recurrent or metastatic squamous cancer of the head and neck randomised to either single agent pembrolizumab immunotherapy or standard of care confirmed an overall survival benefit with immunotherapy from 6.9 to 8.4 months.

A meta-analysis of 1345 patients from 3 RCTs demonstrated better overall survival with anti PD1/PDL1 single agent therapy compared to standard of care chemotherapy in relapsed squamous cancer of head and neck.

A randomized trial found that giving dexamethasone perioperatively for patients undergoing microvascular reconstruction for head and neck cancer had significantly higher mortality (22% vs 5%, p = 0.04 at 12 months, NNTH = 6).

A study compared gemcitabine and cisplatin as induction chemotherapy plus concurrent chemoradiotherapy with concurrent chemoradiotherapy alone in 480 patients with locoregionally advanced nasopharyngeal carcinoma. Overall survival was significantly higher with induction chemotherapy (94.6% vs 90.3%, HR 0.43, 95% CI 0.24 to 0.77). Adverse events were more common with induction but not grade 3 or 4 events.
There is moderate-certainty evidence that elective neck dissection of clinically negative neck nodes reduces the likelihood of recurrence compared with therapeutic neck dissection.

A large randomised controlled trial (n = 596) of the role of elective neck dissection was published in 2015 suggesting improved overall and disease free survival. This has been challenged by a key publication in 2016 which demonstrated that PET-CT surveillance at 12 weeks after chemoradiation enabled neck dissection to be restricted to only those who had active residual disease, thereby sparing unnecessary surgery in many and achieving the same overall survival.
Fluorescence visualization during surgery did not improve outcomes in a randomized trial with 443 patients.

A trial randomized 279 patients with oropharyngeal cancer to neck lymph node dissection or sentinel node biopsy. After 5 years mortality and disease free survival were equivalent, but there was less short term (6 month) morbidy with sentinel node dissection.
In patients with head and neck cancer, progressive resistance therapy is more effective than standard physical therapy for treatment of shoulder dysfunction secondary to therapy.

A systematic review of 8 studies found some evidence to support an association between oral rehabilitation and improved quality of life, although the results of studies were mixed and generally of low quality.

While depression is associated with worse survival among patients with head and neck cancer, it is not clear whether treatment of depression will improve outcomes. Reverse causality, with worse disease or prognosis causing depression, is also possible.
Smoking cessation should be strongly encouraged, although is challenging to establish with failure even with financial incentivisation.

Patients with stage I and stage II tumors are usually treated with radiotherapy alone. Surgery for early stage lesions can be considered, but due to the potential for morbidity and the likelihood of adjuvant radiation therapy, this strategy is not preferred.
Patients with stage III to IVA tumors are treated with concurrent chemotherapy and radiation therapy. Surgery is usually reserved for salvage. NCCN guidelines provide detailed guidance.
Radiotherapy dose reduction or omission of chemotherapy for HPV-positive tumors is considered investigational.

A study randomized 111 patients to 7 days a week accelerated post-operative radiotherapy or postoperative radio-chemotherapy. The latter resulted in improved locoregional control but had no effect on overall survival.

Neoadjuvant chemotherapy prior to definitive treatment with concurrent radiation and chemotherapy is also considered investigational. A systematic review found evidence to support improved survival in patients receiving chemotherapy in addition to radiation and surgery.

Patients with distant metastasis may be treated with palliative systemic chemotherapy or radiation therapy for local control of symptomatic disease. A systematic review found that chemotherapy improved survival somewhat even in patients with unresectable tumors.
There is moderate certainty evidence that there is no difference between PET-CT after chemoradiotherapy compared withplanned neck dissection.
Patients with change in voice or dysphagia should be referred to an ENT surgeon for further evaluation.
Complete dental evaluation for possible tooth extraction prior to therapy should be considered.
Superior outcomes are seen in young, nonsmoking, patients with HPV-positive tumors, while older patients with significant tobacco exposure have worse outcomes.B
The 5 years overall survival by stage: is approximately 80% for localized disease (stage I-II), 50% for regional disease (stage III-IVB), and 15% for metastatic disease (stage IVC). B
The most common route of spread is through the regional lymph node with ipsilateral jugulodigastric node and other level 2 and 3 nodes being involved most often.
Superior outcomes are seen in young, nonsmoking, patients with HPV-positive tumors, while older patients with significant tobacco exposure have worse outcomes.
The 5 years overall survival by stage: is approximately 80% for localized disease (stage I-II), 50% for regional disease (stage III-IVB), and 15% for metastatic disease (stage IVC).
Patients with prior history of a head and neck cancer are considered a high risk population for developing a second primary tumor of the aerodigestive tract.

Even in patients who are cured of their original cancer, some studies have suggested as much as a 20% lifetime risk of developing a second head and neck primary. The yearly risk for developing a second primary has been estimated at 4% to 6% for at least the first 8 years after the original diagnosis.

In patients with previous head and neck cancer, the NCCN recommends a yearly chest x-ray and a physical examination every 1 to 3 months in year one, every 2 to 4 months in year two, every 4 to 6 months in year three to five and every 6 to 12 months in year five and beyond to assess for new or recurrent disease.
It is unclear whether surveillance for plasma and saliva HPV DNA following treatment of low risk patients may lead to earlier diagnosis of recurrence and improve outcome.
